The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let a finite Markov decision process have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, with $d\ge1$. A **differentiable stationary policy family** on $U$ is a family of probabilities $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$, indexed by $\theta\in U$, $s\in S$, and $a\in A(s)$, such that $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=1$, each map $\theta\mapsto\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ is totally differentiable, and for each $s$ there is a fixed nonempty support $B(s)\subseteq A(s)$ with $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)>0$ for every $a\in B(s)$ and $\theta\in U$, while $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=0$ for every $a\notin B(s)$ and $\theta\in U$. The **score vector** at a supported state-action pair is

$$\psi_\theta(s,a):=\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s),\qquad a\in B(s),$$

where the gradient is the Euclidean vector of partial derivatives. The fixed-support condition makes this logarithm defined throughout $U$ on every action that can be sampled.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty state set $S$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Fix an initial state $s_0\in S$ and let

$$Z=\{(s,a,r,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ r\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$$

with its discrete sigma-algebra. There is a probability law on $S\times Z^{\mathbb N}$ whose first state is $S_0=s_0$ and whose subsequent coordinates are $Z_n=(S_n,A_n,R_{n+1},S_{n+1})$. For every $m\ge0$ and every feasible finite trajectory $(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{m-1},r_m,s_m)$, its probability is

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\pi(a_n\mid s_n)\,p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a_n),
$$

where the empty product for $m=0$ is $1$.

Its state-reward marginal also has the finite-prefix probabilities

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\sum_{a\in A(s_n)}\pi(a\mid s_n)p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a)
$$

for each feasible finite state-reward path $(s_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,r_m,s_m)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

If $f,g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ are totally differentiable at $a$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$ and $cf$ are totally differentiable at $a$, with

$$D(f+g)(a)=Df(a)+Dg(a),\qquad D(cf)(a)=cDf(a).$$

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
([[def-equinumerous]]), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of [[def-finite-sum]] when the
values are real and of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]] when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
[[lem-finite-sum-permutation-invariance]] to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
([[def-finite-cardinality]]), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of [[lem-nat-finite-sum-laws-and-the-canonical-embedding]]
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-canonical-natural]]).

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Assume AC for the path laws defining policy values. For a stationary policy $\sigma$, an episode starting from $s$ ends at its first hitting time $T=\inf\{n\ge0:S_n\in S_\dagger\}$; require $T<\infty$ almost surely under every policy used. The return from time $t<T$ is

$$
G_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\gamma^{k-t}R_{k+1},
$$

and $G_T=0$. This equals the infinite discounted return of the absorbing extension, whose state value is $V^\sigma(s)=\mathbb E_{\sigma,s}[G_0]$.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Write $\operatorname{bin}(n)$ for the canonical binary numeral of $n$, with
$\operatorname{bin}(0)=0$. For a binary word $w$, let
$$ c(w):=1^{|w|}0w. $$

For a finite sequence of natural numbers
$$ a=(a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}), $$
define its **sequence word**
$$ W(a):=1\,1^k0\,c(\operatorname{bin}(a_0))\cdots c(\operatorname{bin}(a_{k-1})). $$
The leading $1$ keeps the whole word a canonical positive binary numeral even
when $k=0$.

The **natural-number code** of $a$ is the unique natural number
$$ \ulcorner a\urcorner_{\mathrm{seq}} $$
whose binary numeral is $W(a)$. In particular, the empty sequence has code
$\ulcorner()\urcorner_{\mathrm{seq}}=2$, because $W(())=10$.

By [[lem-finite-tuples-admit-effective-prefix-free-encodings]], the tuple of
binary numerals inside $W(a)$ is effectively and uniquely decodable, so this
construction gives an injective coding of finite sequences of natural numbers
by natural numbers.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Fix an initial state and a terminal set $S_\dagger\subseteq S$. Define $\psi_t=0$ when $t\ge T$. Then, coordinate by coordinate,

$$\mathbb E_\theta[\psi_t\mid\mathcal H_t]=0\quad\text{almost surely for every }t\ge0.$$

The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Expand $R_\gamma=\sum_{k<T}\gamma^kR_{k+1}$. For each $k<t$, the event $t<T$ and the past reward $R_{k+1}$ are $\mathcal H_t$-measurable. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite Markov decision process have nonempty finite state set $S$, finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$, finite reward set $\mathcal R$, and fixed joint transition-reward masses $p(s',r\mid s,a)$. Fix an initial state $s_0\in S$, a terminal set $S_\dagger\subseteq S$, and $0\le\gamma<1$. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $\theta_0\in U$, and let $\pi_\theta$ be a differentiable stationary policy family with fixed common support on an open neighborhood $U_0$ of $\theta_0$. Suppose every episode from $s_0$ under $\pi_\theta$, for $\theta\in U_0$, reaches $S_\dagger$ in finite time almost surely. Let $T$ be the first terminal time, let

$$G_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\gamma^{k-t}R_{k+1}\quad(t<T),\qquad G_T=0,$$

and set $J(\theta)=V^{\pi_\theta}(s_0)=\mathbb E_\theta[\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\gamma^kR_{k+1}]$. Let $\mathcal T$ be the set of finite trajectories that use only actions in the common policy support, have positive transition masses, and stop at their first terminal state. For $\tau=(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{m-1},r_m,s_m)\in\mathcal T$, define

$$p_\theta(\tau)=\prod_{t=0}^{m-1}\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)p(s_{t+1},r_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t),\qquad R_\gamma(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\gamma^kr_{k+1}.$$

Assume the trajectory masses $p_\theta(\tau)$ are totally differentiable at $\theta_0$, the linear map $h\mapsto\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal T}R_\gamma(\tau)Dp_{\theta_0}(\tau)h$ is defined by an absolutely convergent sum, and there is a summable $H:\mathcal T\to[0,\infty)$ that dominates the return-weighted normalized remainders below and for which those remainders tend to zero pathwise:

$$\frac{|R_\gamma(\tau)|\,|p_{\theta_0+h}(\tau)-p_{\theta_0}(\tau)-Dp_{\theta_0}(\tau)h|}{\|h\|_2}\le H(\tau),\qquad \frac{|R_\gamma(\tau)|\,|p_{\theta_0+h}(\tau)-p_{\theta_0}(\tau)-Dp_{\theta_0}(\tau)h|}{\|h\|_2}\longrightarrow0$$

for every $\tau\in\mathcal T$ as $h\to0$, with $\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal T}H(\tau)<\infty$.

Also assume

$$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\!\left[\sum_{t<T}\sum_{k<T}\gamma^k\|\psi_{\theta_0}(S_t,A_t)\|_2\,|R_{k+1}|\right]<\infty,$$

where $\psi_\theta(s,a)=\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ on the common support. Then $J$ is totally differentiable at $\theta_0$ and

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta_0)=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_{\theta_0}(A_t\mid S_t)\,G_t\right].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set, let each $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set, and let $p(s',r\mid s,a)$ be a fixed normalized joint law for the next state and reward. Fix an initial state and a terminal set $S_\dagger\subseteq S$. Under a differentiable stationary policy family with a support that is fixed and strictly positive on that support throughout its open parameter domain, assume the induced episode terminates almost surely. For $t\ge0$, let $\mathcal H_t=\sigma(S_0,A_0,R_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},R_t,S_t)$ be the information available just before the time-$t$ action, and let $\psi_t=\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(A_t\mid S_t)$ when $t<T$, where $T$ is the first terminal time. Define $\psi_t=0$ when $t\ge T$. Then, coordinate by coordinate,

$$\mathbb E_\theta[\psi_t\mid\mathcal H_t]=0\quad\text{almost surely for every }t\ge0.$$

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let a finite Markov decision process have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, with $d\ge1$. A **differentiable stationary policy family** on $U$ is a family of probabilities $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$, indexed by $\theta\in U$, $s\in S$, and $a\in A(s)$, such that $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=1$, each map $\theta\mapsto\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ is totally differentiable, and for each $s$ there is a fixed nonempty support $B(s)\subseteq A(s)$ with $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)>0$ for every $a\in B(s)$ and $\theta\in U$, while $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=0$ for every $a\notin B(s)$ and $\theta\in U$. The **score vector** at a supported state-action pair is

$$\psi_\theta(s,a):=\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s),\qquad a\in B(s),$$

where the gradient is the Euclidean vector of partial derivatives. The fixed-support condition makes this logarithm defined throughout $U$ on every action that can be sampled.

Let a finite MDP have $0\le\gamma<1$ and let $S_\dagger\subseteq S$ be a set of terminal states. Form an absorbing extension with reward alphabet $\mathcal R^\dagger=\mathcal R\cup\{0\}$: from each nonterminal state retain the original joint reward-transition law, and from each terminal state use the deterministic transition back to that state with reward zero. Assume AC for the path laws defining policy values. For a stationary policy $\sigma$, an episode starting from $s$ ends at its first hitting time $T=\inf\{n\ge0:S_n\in S_\dagger\}$; require $T<\infty$ almost surely under every policy used. The return from time $t<T$ is

$$
G_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\gamma^{k-t}R_{k+1},
$$

and $G_T=0$. This equals the infinite discounted return of the absorbing extension, whose state value is $V^\sigma(s)=\mathbb E_{\sigma,s}[G_0]$.

For a state-value estimate $V_n$, the state temporal-difference error on a transition is $\delta_n^V=R_{n+1}+\gamma V_n(S_{n+1})-V_n(S_n)$. For an action-value estimate $Q_n$, the sampled-action Sarsa error is $\delta_n^{\mathrm{Sarsa}}=R_{n+1}+\gamma Q_n(S_{n+1},A_{n+1})-Q_n(S_n,A_n)$, and the greedy Q-learning error is $\delta_n^{Q}=R_{n+1}+\gamma\max_{b\in A(S_{n+1})}Q_n(S_{n+1},b)-Q_n(S_n,A_n)$. In each error, the continuation term is defined as zero when $S_{n+1}$ is terminal.

In off-policy prediction, $\mu$ denotes the behavior policy generating episodes and $\pi$ the target policy whose value is estimated. Target support means $\pi(a\mid s)>0$ implies $\mu(a\mid s)>0$ for every state-action pair that can be visited. For a behavior-generated episode, the state-return likelihood ratio from time $t$ is

$$
\Lambda_{t:T-1}=\prod_{k=t}^{T-1}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{\mu(A_k\mid S_k)}.
$$

Each denominator is positive on the observed behavior path. When estimating a value conditional on an already fixed action $A_t$, the first factor begins at time $t+1$.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then

$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

citations.quote:
Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let a finite Markov decision process have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, with $d\ge1$. A **differentiable stationary policy family** on $U$ is a family of probabilities $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$, indexed by $\theta\in U$, $s\in S$, and $a\in A(s)$, such that $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=1$, each map $\theta\mapsto\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ is totally differentiable, and for each $s$ there is a fixed nonempty support $B(s)\subseteq A(s)$ with $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)>0$ for every $a\in B(s)$ and $\theta\in U$, while $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)=0$ for every $a\notin B(s)$ and $\theta\in U$. The **score vector** at a supported state-action pair is

$$\psi_\theta(s,a):=\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s),\qquad a\in B(s),$$

where the gradient is the Euclidean vector of partial derivatives. The fixed-support condition makes this logarithm defined throughout $U$ on every action that can be sampled.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$
